They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "Let's make it a game and see who can make the noise that scares the seals the most."

They made different noises, but nothing worked. Then one of the young men said, "I have an idea. Let me try making a noise like a baby seal."

As soon as he made the noise, a seal popped its head out of the water and looked around. The two young men crept closer and closer until they could see directly into the seal's eyes. The seal was so frightened that it jumped out of the water and landed on the ice.

The two young men cheered and high-fived each other. "You really stumbled upon something," one of them said. "Yes, it's amazing," the other replied. "Let's try something like that again."

They spent the rest of the night making baby seal noises and scaring seals. They were so excited that they forgot to even take a look at the foggy scenery.

The sun began to rise and the two young men went back to their village. They were tired but happy. "That was incredible!" one of them said. "Yes, it was," the other agreed. "Let's go back to the river and make some more baby seal noises."

They went back to the river every night after that and scared seals with their baby seal noises. And sometimes, when it was really quiet, they would listen to the peaceful sounds of the river and the fog.

They heard a voice calling them, but they could not tell where the call was coming from. They looked around but could not see anything. Suddenly, a great wave came up and washed them away.

Analysis
This story is one of several from the Tlingit collection of oral traditions that involve supernatural beings who live in the rivers and bodies of water. In this story, the two young men are hunting seals, which are also supernatural beings in the Tlingit worldview. The fog and calm suggest the transition from the natural world to the supernatural world, and the great wave that washes them away is probably a manifestation of the Tlingit concept of Hédi, the supernatural force that is both creator and destroying of the universe.

It is an example of a type of Tlingit story known as a transformational story, in which a human being is transformed into an animal or a supernatural being, or vice versa. In this story, the two young men are transformed into ghosts.

== Translation ==
Once upon a time

They heard a strange noise, and one of them said it was an ork, or wind. As they were traveling home early in the morning, they came across a strange sight - a number of humans moving slowly and quietly along the shore. The men from Egulac had never seen humans before, and they were afraid. They turned and ran away as fast as they could.
The humans were actually members of a party from the Red Creek Potlatch, returning to their homes after a feast. They were carrying lit torches, which is why the men from Egulac could not see their faces, and why they moved so quietly - they were silent on the theory that noise would disturb the spirits.

Origins
This story is one of many collected by Francis Bernice Krause in the early 20th century about the early encounters between indigenous people of the northwest coast of America and Europeans. It is a variation on the theme of the "Strange People from the South", a common motif in the oral traditions of many Native American tribes.

Symbolism
In this story, the fog could represent the mist that often descends in the Pacific Northwest. The seal hunters are unnamed in the story, but one of them is described as having a cauldron tattooed on his forehead. This may represent his position as a shaman or healer. The fact that he is the one who hears the strange noise may indicate that he is particularly receptive to the supernatural.

They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "Let's make sure it's safe and not a killer whale." That's when they noticed a seal nearby. The men were from Egulac, a village on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island within the Heiltsuk First Nation territory. This story is one of many that are part of an oral history that was passed down to the present-day Heiltsuk people. The history is filled with stories of the early days of mining on the island and the role that the Heiltsuk people played in the industry.

Mining on Vancouver Island
The concept of mining on Vancouver Island began in the 1800s and was well underway by the early 1900s. According to the Canadian Encyclopedia, "More than 750 mines and prospect sites are recorded on Vancouver Island and its coastal islands." Some of the mines were productive for only a decade or two, while others had a life span of 50 years or more. The mines were scattered throughout the island, although the majority were located in the northwest.The mineral resources on Vancouver Island were a major factor in the economic development of the province. The mines provided employment for hundreds of men and brought wealth to the area. However, the mining operations often disturbing the landscape and were often unsafe. Many of the mines used mercury, a highly toxic substance, in the processing of their ores. Mercury contamination is a major environmental concern by, and was even listed by the United States Environmental Protection Agency as a Superfund site.

They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "That's the sound of the sea being torn apart." They went to investigate and saw a piece of rock falling from the cliff into the sea. They ran back to Egulac and warned the people there to move to higher ground before the tsunami came.

Prehistoric tsunami
This is possibly the earliest recorded tsunami warning in history, and certainly predates any written records. The people of Egulac were aware that a large wave was on its way and had time to warn their fellow villagers to move to higher ground before the wave struck. The warning was passed from person to person until it reached the village of Adamstown where the mayor was alerted and he ordered an evacuation. Since the 19th century, this type of warning has become commonplace along the coasts of British Columbia.

Tsunami
The tsunami that was caused by the landslide in 1847 was one of the largest recorded in North America. It was seen and felt as far south as San Francisco. The wave entered and destroyed the then-extensive salt-water lagoon at Bella Bella. The massive wave was reported as high as 1,000 feet (300 m) high when it hit Egulac.

Aftermath
One person was reported dead in Egulac. This was possibly the earliest recorded fatality from a tsunami. After the wave had passed, the people of Egulac went to the site of the landslide and found the body of a man they had suspected was buried there. They moved the body to higher ground and then waited for the next wave. When nothing happened, they went down to the shore to recover their vessels and bury the dead man.

The story
This story is one of several tales told by the Kwakiutl people, an indigenous people of the northwest coast of North America, to explain the strange noises heard in nature. In this tale, the sound of the inland sea is personified as a living being.
The story is told as a part of the Tale of the Four Brothers. In this tale, four brothers go out in a canoe to hunt seals. The first brother is told to watch the canoe, the second to watch the land, the third to watch the sea, and the fourth to watch the sky. The brother who is watching the sea hears the sound of the inland sea and tells the others what he has seen, but they do not believe him. Later, when a great wave comes and swamps the canoe, they all begin to call out to the inland sea for help, but it does not come. Finally, they all jump overboard and swim to safety on the shore, but the fourth brother is swept away by the sea.

Symbolism
The tale of the four brothers is a coming of age story, a rite of passage story, a story of discovery and of the unknown. The unknown can be scary, but it can also be full of wonder and amazement. In this story, the unknown is personified as the inland sea, a great and powerful force that is both beautiful and terrifying.
The brothers in this story represent the different parts of a person's character: the watcher, the protector, the explorer, and the dreamer. We all have these parts within us, and they can sometimes be in conflict. But when we learn to balance these parts of ourselves, we can live a rich and fulfilling life.

But a few days later, when the fog lifted and everyone was able to see what had happened, it turned out that the voice they had heard was not Wilfie's at all. It had been the voice of one of the village elders, who had been trying to warn them of the danger of hunting in the fog.

The story of the three young men from Egulac is a story of friendship and bravery, but it is also a warning. It reminds us that sometimes the things we value most highly – our friends, our community, our life – can be endangered in mysterious and unexpected ways. And when that happens, we may need to act quickly and bravely, even if we don't have all the information we need. We may even need to trust our instincts, our feelings, and our relationships, even if they don't make complete sense to us at the time.

This story is from the Tlingit people.

It is a cautionary tale, warning of the approaching Euro-American contact and the changes that it would bring. The tale is often told in conjunction with the story of the otter woman, who appears when people are in need.

Tlingit stories
Tlingit stories are passed down from generation to generation by word of mouth. They are stories of the natural world, of creation, of heroes and tricksters, and of the spirit world. Tlingit stories are often told in cycles, with each story leading to the next. They are told in a special tone, with a rhythm and pace that reflects the nature of the story. Tlingit stories are more than just tales; they are a way of preserving the Tlingit culture and world view. They are a means of passing on the knowledge, wisdom, and traditions of the Tlingit people.

The Song of the Sea
The Song of the Sea is a rare natural phenomenon that occurs on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island in Canada. It is a tidal singer, a phenomenon where the tidal waters sing a song as the water moves in and out of the narrow straits between the islands and the mainland. The effect is heightened in times of fog, when the cool moisture condenses on the cold air over the warmer water, creating a distinctive, haunting melody.
The phenomenon is not unique to this area; similar occurrences have been reported in the Bay of Exploits in Newfoundland and in Strait of Juan de Fuca in the north of Vancouver Island.

They heard a strange cry, and it seemed to them that it was crying: "Egulac, Egulac." They looked at one another and were afraid, and they fled to the hills. Later they told the people of Egulac that it had been a bad dream, but they knew that it was true that they had heard the cry "Egulac, Egulac."

The people of Egulac decided that they would go and find out where the cry was coming from. They picked a day when the tide was high and everyone went down to the beach. They started to search for the source of the cry, but because it was foggy and calm, they could not find anything. They called out: "Egulac, where are you?" but nothing happened.

Then one of the younger men spoke up: "Let us go and ask the old people in the village." And they did. The old people told them: "Long ago, when we were young, we used to come down to the beach and cry out: 'Egulac, Egulac.' And we would then throw sticks into the water and make believe that we were fighting our enemies. That is where the cry came from."

From that day on, whenever the people of Egulac went down to the beach, they would cry out: "Egulac, Egulac." And they would throw sticks into the water and make believe that they were fighting their enemies. And even to this day, if you go down to the beach at Egulac, you will sometimes hear the cry: "Egulac, Egulac." And you will see the people of Egulac throwing sticks into the water.

They heard a cry for help. It came from a woman who was being held by a man in a canoe on the other side of the river. The woman begged them to come and help her, but they were afraid. They didn't want to go out into the fog, where they couldn't see, and might get lost. But the woman kept crying for help, and finally the two young men decided to go and see what was happening. They went out into the fog, and followed the sound of the woman's cries until they came to the edge of a cliff. There they saw a man holding a woman, and as they approached, he let her go and jumped off the cliff himself. The woman was grateful, and from that day on, the two young men were known as brave heroes who had saved her. As a reward, she gave them each a kiss, and they lived happily ever after.

Notes
This story is from the Tlingit tribe of the Pacific Northwest coast. It is a variation on the theme of the hero who saves a damsel in distress, with the twist that the hero does not initially want to help. Instead, he is afraid of the unknown. This fear is depicted as an instinctual fear, a fear of getting lost or falling off a cliff. The story shows that sometimes people have to overcome their fears and act bravely, even when they don't feel brave.

The woman
Many versions of this story exist, and in some the woman is not a chief's daughter but the chief's wife, who has been seduced by a stranger and is now pregnant. In others, it is the stranger himself who speaks to the young men, begging them to kill him and spare his shame.

The message
The message the young men took back to the chief is also important. In one version, it is a rock with a piece of turquoise set into it. In another, it is a bundle of the chief's hair. In yet another, it is a bundle of arrows, one for each month of the pregnancy.

The aftermath
In some versions, the chief is so angry with his daughter/wife that he banishes her/them from the village forever. In others, he is so proud of her/their bravery that he welcomes them back with open arms.

Commentary
This story illustrates the idea that there are some things that should not be seen or heard. It shows that there are boundaries that should not be crossed, and that people have the right to practice their own beliefs without fear of interference or disrespect. It is also an example of the idea that sometimes it is better not to know something. In this story, the two men were happier not knowing what they had heard.

There exist variant folktales of this story, where the two young men are either  from the Tlingit or the Haida tribe. Origin
This story probably originated after the contact with the Europeans, possibly as a result of the fur trade. In this story, the foghorn represented the natural environment and the warnings it gave were ignored, with disastrous consequences.

The voice had come from the mouth of the Raven River, and as they looked closer, they saw a pile of old bones. It was the skeleton of a woman, and as they investigated further, they found a piece of paper in her pocket. It was a map to a nearby island, and on that island there was a burial ground. The men were sure that this was the burial ground of a Tlingit woman and they respectfully placed the bones in a box and took them to the village burial ground.
The next day the men went back to the Raven River to continue their hunt for seals. They had almost reached the same spot when they heard a voice again, but this time it was clear that it was coming from the water. They looked around for a hidden mouth of a river or a place where the water could be coming from, but they saw nothing. Suddenly, a ring of mist formed in the air and out of the fog came a handmade wooden canoe. In the canoe was a Tlingit woman, rowing toward the men with a pale face.
The men were shocked and afraid, but the woman did not seem to notice. She came closer and closer until she was only a few feet away. She spoke to the men in a voice that was soft and sad. She told them that she had died in childbirth and that her baby had been

They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "Let's go home, that's a bad sign." But the other said, "No, it's only the river. Let's keep on." Suddenly, a great wave rose in the midst of the fog, and they were drowned.

Analysis
This story is from the Tlingit tribe of the northwest coast of Canadian and American Pacific coasts. It is a reminder of the unpredictable nature of the sea and the respect mariners should have for it. The story is also an example of the type of tales that can be told around a campfire.

They made a noise and threw rocks and logs in the air. But the train just kept coming closer and closer. It was a westbound CPR train with a head of steam. After the collision

They heard a strange sound, but did not pay much attention to it. Suddenly, they saw a light moving on the water. It was coming towards them. When it got closer, they could see that it was a canoe, but nobody was steering it. The canoe hit them, and when they looked up, they saw that the canoe was being swung around by a giant octopus. The two young men tried to paddle away, but the octopus grabbed hold of their canoe with two of its tentacles and pulled it under. The fog was so thick that the young men could not see anything. They wanted to go back to Egulac, but they did not know which way to go. They decided to follow the tentacles. They paddled for hours, following the tentacles, but there was still no sign of land. Just as they were beginning to lose hope, they saw a light in the distance. It was a campfire. The young men had finally reached the village of Tladiin. The Chief of Tladiin welcomed them warmly, and asked them about their adventure. They told him everything, including the mysterious fog, the canoe that was pulled by an octopus, and how they had finally reached land by following the tentacles. The Chief listened carefully to their story, and then told them that long ago, before the days of the strong tide, the old villagers had gone out in canoes to hunt seals in the same place, and they too had been pulled under by one of the great octopuses of the sea. From then on, the young men did not go out in canoes when there was fog, and they always followed the tentacles when they were on the water. Tired from their adventure, the two young men lay down by the fire and fell asleep.

They heard a strange sound, and then saw a light coming towards them. It was the light of an oncoming train, and though the train was moving slowly, the men were unable to get out of the way. Both men were struck and killed by the train.

The next morning the body of one of the men was found near the river, but the other man's body could not be found. It was later found several miles down the river, many miles from where the other man had been found.

This story is from the Tsimshian people. In many Tsimshian stories, people are tested by the supernatural. In this story, the two men are tested by the coming of a train, a machine that was supernatural to the Tsimshian. One man is able to avoid danger, but the other is not. The story does not tell us why the two men were out at night, but we can assume that they were up to no good. The train is portrayed as a force of nature, an unstoppable machine that can kill without mercy. The story shows the dangers of being near a moving train, but also shows the importance of being able to make quick decisions and act upon them.

Retrospect
This story is one of several Tsimshian stories that involve trains. In the story, a train is portrayed as a force of nature, an unstoppable machine that can kill without mercy. This is in direct contrast to the way that trains are portrayed in many other Native American stories. For example, in a Navajo story, a train is used as a symbol of freedom and progress. In a Lakota story, a train is used as a symbol of the destructive force of war. In this Tsimshian story, the train is neither good nor evil; it is simply a force to be reckoned with.

Geography
Osooyos Lake is a small lake, about 1.5 km long and 0.5 km wide, with a maximum depth of 32 m. It is located midway up the north side of Okanagan Lake, at an elevation of 475 m above sea level. A mountainous area, it is surrounded by steep cliffs and rocky outcrops. To the west is Quintette Mountain, to the north is Rattlesnake Mountain, and to the south is Mt Henry.

History
The area around Osooyos Lake was inhabited by several First Nations groups, including the Sinixt, Northern Paiute, and Okanagan Indians. The lake is significant historically as the site where, in 1859, the Sinixt people were forced to surrender their land to the Canadian government. The area was made a reserve in 1878, and remained in the hands of the Sinixt people until 1954, when it was sold to a private individual.

They went to the source of the sound and saw that it was coming from a rock. They approached the rock and touched it, and the rock spoke to them. It told them to go back to their families and tell them what they had learned on that journey. It warned them to be careful because the whites were coming. It gave them a new law, the Law of the First Born, and told them that when they went back they would have the strength of ten men. The two young men went back to Egulac and told their families and friends what had happened. They were amazed and asked many questions. The two young men told them everything that had happened, including the new law that had been given to them. From that day on, the people of Egulac lived by the Law of the First Born, and it became a special part of their history.

---
This story is a part of the Métis storytelling tradition, and it tells the story of how the Métis people came to receive the Law of the First Born. This law was said to have been given to the Métis by the rock itself, and it was a source of strength and guidance. The law stated that when the Métis went out into the world, they would have the strength of ten men. This law was important because it helped the Métis people to understand their place in the world and gave them a sense of identity. It also warned them of the dangers that lay ahead, specifically the threat of the 'whites'. The whites were represented by the fog in the story, and they were seen as a force that could obscure the truth and lead people astray. By contrast, the rock represented the truth itself, and it spoke with the voice of authority.

The two men were now stranded on an island in the middle of the Salish Sea with a canoe full of rocks. They paddled towards the mainland, but as they were nearing the shore a great storm arose. They had not completed their hunt and had only taken one seal. The two men were hungry and began to search for food. They looked for berries and roots, but could not find any. Just as they were about to give up, they saw a beaver working at the edge of a marsh. They followed it into the marsh and killed it with a spear. As they were pulling the beaver into their canoe, they heard a voice calling out, "Now you have enough to eat."  The men paddled to the south and east, following the coastline, looking for more food and for a place to shelter for the night. As they rounded a bend in the coast, they saw a village of Tigqua people. They had lived there for many years and had a peaceful life there. The two men went up to the village and asked if they could stay for the night. The Tigquas welcomed them and fed them. They told the men that the fog had been sent by the great chief of the north wind, and that the rocks in the canoe were a sign that the chief was pleased with their hunting. The men spent the night in the village, and the next day they continued on their journey, feeling refreshed and nourished.

Analysis
This is a story about darkness and light, about fear and bravery, about the importance of understanding other people and working together. It is also a story about a monster, or at least a strange and frightening creature. But the monster is not the enemy. The enemy is fear itself, and the story shows how fear can be overcome by bravery and understanding.

Variants
Some versions of the story have the two young men being sent to the mouth of the river by their fathers, who are also told of the danger of going out on the water when it is foggy and calm, but they go anyway. In one version, it is only after the two have drowned that the fog lifts and the fathers are able to see where they have gone. Another version has it that the two were out on the water when a sudden storm came up, with rain, fog, and great waves.

Origins
This story is one of several created to explain the origins of the Egulac people. According to anthropologist Helen Bender, it is likely that this tale is from the Kwiakiutl group of stories. She notes that this story shares certain elements with stories from the northern Kwakiutl and Heiltsuk stories, such as the foggy canvas that covers the sky, the calmness of the water, and the suddenness of the disaster. She also notes that this story has several elements that are also found in stories from the Ojosoye language group, such as the importance of the season and the role of the tide.

Symbolism
The story can be seen as a cautionary tale about the dangers of going out on the water when it is foggy and calm, and how important it is to heed the warnings of the elders. It can also be seen as a tale about the importance of respecting the power of the natural world and understanding one's place in it. The tale can be interpreted on several levels, and can be seen as a reminder of the need for humility and respect for the unknown.

The wave that drowned the two young men was caused by a tide that had been held back by a rock known as the Pylon from the Strait of Egulac. When the tide was let loose, it came crashing down with great force.
The two young men who were drowned were the daughters of the chief of the Egulac tribe, so when the news reached the village, the people were very sad. They held a big funeral, and then they decided to build a house of mourning, known as a "hedger house".
After the house of mourning was built, the people of Egulac did not go out on the water again until the next summer, when they held a big canoe festival. They paddled their canoes out to the place where the two young women had drowned, and then they turned the canoes around and paddled back to the village, carrying the bodies of the two women. They buried them in the cemetery beside the church, and then they went back to the village to continue the festival.
The people of Egulac say that even today, if you go down to the river near the Pylon you can hear the noise that caused the drowning of the two young women. Sometimes, when the tide is coming in, you can see a great wave coming down that looks just like the wave that drowned them. But whatever you do, do not go out on the water when it happens, because that wave is sure to drown you too.

This is the tale of the mythical lake Egulac and the spirit that haunts it. According to the Ktunaxa people, the lake was named after a powerful spirit that lived there. Long ago, a group of hunters had gone out from the village of Kinbasket in the wintertime to hunt for seals on the iced-over lake. It was always foggy and calm at Egulac, even when the rest of the world was blanketted in snow. The hunters had a warm camp on the lake, with a fire burning to keep them comfortable. They heard a strange noise, and one of them said to the other: 'Let us go home; this is not a good place to be when it is foggy and calm.' But the other answered: 'There is nothing to fear; it is only the fog that has come down to the river.'  They continued to hunt and as they were returning home along the bank, the ice broke under them and they both fell into the water. They both drowned and when they were recovered, it was found that they had been drinking. The coroner's jury concluded that they had been killed by the intoxication caused by drinking.

Details
The story is from a collection of tales told by the Tlingit people, and the tale is called "The Two Young Men from Egulac." It is told by the storyteller  as a warning to young people who drink and then go out in a canoe or boat when it is foggy and calm. The story is similar to the English version of the tale called "The Bell Rock Lighthouse."

Explainer
Tlingit stories are passed down through generations by word of mouth, and each tribe has its own version of stories. Tlingit stories are rich in animals and the supernatural. They often explain the world around us, and how things came to be.

Characters
In the story, the two young men are not named. They are just "two young men from Egulac." However, in some versions of the story, they are named Pakuki and Nalini. In other versions, they are named Paksit and Nalinka.

Moral
The moral of the story is that drinking and then going out in a boat when it is foggy and calm is dangerous. It is better to stay home where it is safe.

They built a strong village, and the Wolves of the Wetlands became respected members of the community. The two young men from Egulac were especially respected, as they had learned so much from the Wolves and were now putting that knowledge to use in helping others.
Years later, when the white man came, the Wolves of the Wetlands were among the first to make contact. They shared their knowledge of the area with the white men, and formed alliances that would last for generations.

Albertans probably first learned about the Egulac seal hunt from George Bain's 1882 book, The Heart of the Stoney. In it, he wrote:

Two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals, and while they were there it became foggy and calm. They heard a strange noise, and one of them said: "That's the sound of a witch's charms being thrown into the water." They went home to their wives and told them what they had heard, and they were all afraid. Bain's tale is a variation of a theme found in many cultures, in which humans are warned off by supernatural beings. In this case, the humans are warned not by gods or monster-beings, but by a seemingly benign witch who is actually gathering power for an attack. The warning comes not in a dream or a prophecy, but through direct perception of a red light on the water.

Many Algonquian stories involve hunting, and often the hunt is successful only after the hunters have gained the help of a spirit helper. In some stories, the hunter is warned away from a dangerous encounter. The warning may come from a dream, a prophecy, or a wise old man or woman.

Prior to European contact
The First Nations people who lived in the area before European contact were the Haida, Nootka, Owi, and Kwiakiutl. The Haida and Nootka were semi-nomadic hunter-gatherers who seasonally hunted for seal along the northwest coast of Vancouver Island and the mainland. The Owi and Kwiakiutl were inland hunter-gatherers who hunted for seal as well as other animals such as bear, wolf, and beaver. Seal meat was an important part of their diet and their way of life.

Contact with European settlers
When the Europeans arrived, the Indigenous people showed them how to hunt seals. The early settlers relied on the Haida and Nootka for their survival. The Haida and Nootka taught the settlers how to find and harvest camas, berries, and other plants. They also showed them how to hunt seals, both for their meat and their hides. The settlers soon learned how to hunt seals on their own. They used long spears with a float on the end to keep the spear vertical in the water. A piece of meat was attached to the float to attract the seals. The settlers were successful in their hunting and soon depleted the seal population in the area.

analysis
This story is from the Tlingit people. The moral of the story is not clear without additional context. It is possible that the story is simply intended to explain a natural phenomenon, such as a tidal wave. However, the story may also have a deeper meaning. For example, it is possible that the two young men represent two different reactions to danger: one reaction is to flee, and the other is to stay and fight. Alternatively, the story may be interpreted as a warning against pride and overconfidence. For example, the two young men may be seen as representing the Tlingit people, who were at one time overconfident in their ability to control the natural world.

Seal People
The Egulac people tell a story about the Seal People. Long ago, when the people of Egulac were starving, they decided to ask the Seal People for help. They sent out a party of hunters to catch as many seals as possible. The hunters went out in a canoe and called out to the Seal People, asking them to come and help the people who were dying of hunger. The Seal People heard the cries of the hunters and came rushing to their aid. But when the hunters saw the Seal People, they were afraid and began to fight them. The Seal People were astonished. "Why are you fighting us?" they asked. "We have come to help you." But the hunters were too afraid to stop fighting.
The Seal People saw that the fighting was pointless. "From now on," they said, "we will help you whenever you are in trouble. But if you want to hurt us, we will disappear forever." The hunters agreed to the Seal People's proposal and from that time on the Egulac people had a friendly relationship with the Seal People.

This is the story of the eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980 as told by the Klikitat people. The mountain is located in the Cascade Range in southeastern Washington state, and is one of the most actively volcanic areas in the United States. Although the Klikitat people no longer live in the area, the story is an important part of the regional folklore.
The mountain was named after Saint Helena of Constantinople, the wife of the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great. The name was suggested by the resemblance of the mountain's peak to a woman's breast.
Mount St. Helens is a stratovolcano, one of the most common types of volcanoes in the Cascade Range. It was formed by the accumulation of ash and lava over thousands of years. The peak of the mountain is marked by a pale lavender-colored 

composite cone, which is separated from the main body of the mountain by a topographic dip. The cone is thought to be the remains of an ancient volcano that was active during the first phase of mountain building in the Cascades. The current summit is located at the northern end of a 10 km long fossil rift valley.
The 1980 eruption was the most destructive volcanic episode in the history of Mount St. Helens. It began on May 18, 1980, when a magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered a landslide of rock and ice, which was followed by a year-long series of eruptive events. He told them that long ago, a great flood had passed through the village, carrying away everything in its path, including the bodies of two young men who had foolishly stayed behind. The old man's grandparents had told him the story of how, after the flood, the people found the two bodies trapped under a fallen tree, with the mist from the river fogging up the air and making it seem as if the water itself had drowned them. That was why the villagers had built a house on the spot, so that the two young men would not be alone in the afterworld.

The men were frightened by this story, and decided to stop hunting seals there. From then on, whenever it fogged up and the rippling sound came, the men would remember the two young men who had died in the flood and tell themselves that it was only the mist making the water sound strange. And that is what happened.

In the legend of the Curse of the Egulac, a wealthy and powerful tribe of native people lived along the shore of the sea. They were the Egulac. They had peacefully lived on the land for hundreds of years when a group of explorers from a far-off land came and took possession of the land, pushing the Egulac people into the mountains. The explorers built a railroad along the shore so that they could easily transport their stolen goods back to their own land. The Egulac people cursed the railroad and predicted that as long as the line of track remained on their land, their people would never know peace.

The curse and the train
It is said that the curse brought disaster upon the railroad. Many believe that it was the curse that caused the train to go off the rails that night. Some say that it was a mistake by the engineer that caused the disaster, but no one knows for certain. What is certain is that from that night on the Egulac people refused to have anything to do with the railroad and warned others to stay away as well.

The aftermath
The warning was ignored and soon other incidents occurred that proved to be even more disastrous. In 1872, a train fell into the sea near the same spot, drowning all aboard. They heard a strange noise, and one of them said to the other: "That's the sound of the ocean turning over."

This is a story from the Tlingit people, one of the many groups of Native Americans who lived along the Pacific coast of North America. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The story appears in the compilation of Native American stories and legends called "Tlingit Indian Stories," edited by John P. Buchanan. The story is told in the form of a dialogue between two hunters, named Egula and Chissun. At the end of the story, it is unclear whether the hunters survived the encounter with the turning over ocean.

Interpretation
The story of the turning over ocean is a literal interpretation of a natural phenomenon. In the story, the ocean is personified as a living being that is conscious and can make decisions. The idea of the ocean "turning over" could be a metaphor for a number of things, including a change in season, a change in the weather, or a change in the natural order of things. It could also be a warning of an impending disaster.

Symbolism
In Tlingit culture, the ocean is a powerful and spiritual force. It is the source of life, and is respected and honored. The ocean is also a powerful symbol of change and transformation. It can represent the unknown, the mysterious, and the spiritual realm.

Origin
The story of the turning over ocean is believed to have originated among the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest. The exact origin is unknown, as the story was passed down orally from generation to generation.

Other versions
Other versions of this story include a warning to sailors to stay away from the coast when the ocean is "turning over." In one version, the punishment for disobeying the warning is death. In another version, the penalty is blindness.

== Origin ==
This story is from the Tlingit people. The Tlingit people are one of the many Native American tribes of the Northwest Coast. Their homeland is the Tlingit Gyaaxáda, which refers to the original territory of the Tlingit people. The Tlingit people are known for their strong work ethic and their ability to adapt to new situations. They are also known for their storytelling, art, and their deep respect for the natural world.

== Symbolism ==
In this story, the Megamerlin represents the natural world. The tasks given by the serpent represent the challenges we face in life. The trout represent the things we value, such as family and friends. The green snake represents jealousy. The story tells us that in order to be successful and happy, we must work hard and face our challenges head on. We must also be aware of the potential for jealousy and other negative emotions.

The native people of this area are usually referred to as the Chinook because of their prominent trade in salmon and steelhead fish. The Chinook traded these fish with neighboring tribes for other resources, such as clams and berries. The Chinook people were also known for their canoes, which were used for trading and for traveling.

The Chinook people were the first Native American group to establish a relationship with early European explorers and traders. The native people of the area showed great curiosity towards the newcomers and allowed them to observe their ways of life. Story origin
This story is from the Tlingit people, who live (and originally came from) along the northwest coast of British Columbia and the southeast coast of Alaska. The story can be found in the collection of Tlingit stories called "The Wisdom of the Elders", which was compiled by Robert J. Ficklin.

This story can be seen as a warning not to go out on the water when there is a fog. It can also be seen as a story that explains the origin of a group of people. This is a common theme in Tlingit stories. Another theme in this story is the idea of sacrifice. The two young men sacrifice their lives in order to help the crew of the wrecked ship. They followed the sound until they came to a piece of land where there was a hollow tree. They looked inside and saw hundreds of little creatures, like mice, scurrying around. This story is a part of the Métis storytelling tradition, a oral storytelling tradition passed down through generations. == Transcription == 
Two Young Men from Egulac

Once upon a time, two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. They had a little boat, and they took it out to the middle of the river, where the tidal current is very strong.

It was getting foggy and calm, and they were sitting there waiting for the tide to turn when suddenly a great wave came up and struck their little boat. They rowed hard to get away from the wave, but the current was too strong. It took them. It drowned them.

The next morning, when the fog lifted, they found the bodies of the two young men floating in the river.

Once upon a time, long ago, two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was a foggy, calm night. They had a little boat, and in that boat they had a lantern to light their way. They were out on the river near the big bluff, K'ust Tlu, when suddenly the sky grew dim and the stars disappeared. Then they saw a light coming toward them, growing bigger and bigger until it shone everywhere around them. It was the light of Megami, the great sea monster. She could see the young men clearly even though it was pitch dark outside. She opened her mouth wide and swallowed them up.

The Egulac People and the Sea Monster
The people of Egulac mourned the loss of the two young men. They were very sad. But they did not give up hope. They decided to set a trap for the sea monster. They built a huge round trap with strong ropes and sturdy logs. They waited and watched for Megami. Finally, one night they saw her coming towards them, her eyes glowing in the dark. She was so huge that the water around her was turbulent and noisy. The people shouted and waved their arms to scare her away from the trap. Megami hesitated for a moment, then plunged back into the water. The people quickly closed the trap and secured it with extra ropes. They cheered and danced, knowing they had captured the sea monster.

Seal hunting
In the late 1800s and early 1900s, seals were a valuable resource for the people of Egulac and the other villages along the northwest coast of British Columbia. Seal meat was a protein source and their hides were used to make clothing and other articles. The fur trade was important to the native people and helped establish a trading relationship with the European settlers.

Fog
Fog is a common occurrence in the Egulac area. Dense fog can roll in quickly from the sea, obscuring vision and making travel difficult. Sometimes the fog is so thick that it feels like rain. In the native Tlingit language the term for fog is "hina".

Legend
The legend of the two young men who went hunting on the foggy night and drowned is a well-known tale among the Tlingit people. The story is a cautionary tale about the dangers of venturing out on the water when there is fog. The tale is often told to children to teach them to respect the power of nature.

The story is told in the novel "Babi Wai" by Robert C. Thomas, Jr., which was published in 1997. The title of the book is the Tlingit name for the coastal city of Victoria, British Columbia.

Background
The Tlingit people are one of the three main First Nations groups that inhabit the northwest coast of British Columbia and Alaska. The other two groups are the Haida and the Kwakiutl. The Tlingit people were the most aggressive of the three groups in defending their traditional territories from outsiders. At one point, the Tlingit people had control of almost the entire northwest coast of British Columbia and Alaska. The Tlingit people are known for their wood carvings, which are some of the most intricate and detailed in North America. Tlingit carvings can be found in many museums and private collections around the world.

The men were fascinated by her, and they asked her who she was. "I am the Morning Star," she replied. "I come from the heavens to bring light to the world." The men were overwhelmed by her beauty, and they begged her to stay with them. She agreed to stay, on one condition. "You must build a house for me," she said. "And when the time comes, you must light a great bonfire and gather all the wise men of the country. I will give them my wisdom, and they will pass it on to future generations." The men agreed to her condition, and they built a beautiful house on the shore. The woman stayed there, and she brought light and wisdom to the world. But she warned the men that there would come a time when people would forget her teachings and live only for themselves. "When that happens," she said, "you must light the bonfire again and call me back from the heavens."

Analysis
This is a story about the fear of the unknown. The two young men are out hunting, which is an ordinary activity, but when they encounter the monster, their fear overwhelms them. The monster's appearance is described in terms that make it clear that this is an extraordinary creature, one that the young men have never seen before. Their reaction is to run away as fast as they can, back to their homes in Egulac.

Characters
The two young men are not named in the story, and we do not learn anything about them. We know that they are from Egulac, and that they go hunting seals, but beyond that, we do not know anything about them. The monster is also unnamed, and we know nothing about it, other than the fact that it is huge, has long horns, and glowing red eyes.

Symbolism
The fog that covers the river could symbolize the fog of uncertainty that surrounds the unknown. The monster could represent the unknown itself, something that is vast and terrifying. The fact that the monster has no name and is not defined in any way shows that it is a symbol of the unknown.

Explanation
The story is set in the Egulac village of the Kwakiutl ancestral people of the First Nations of Canada. The specific story is from the Tsimshian people. The story is told in various versions in the Tsimshian, Kwakiutl, and Haida nations. The Haida people tell a version of the story in which the two young men are transformed into thunderbirds.

Symbolism
The story can be seen as a metaphor for the struggle of the First Nations people to breathe in a world dominated by outsiders. The fog can represent the confusion of the world and the calm water represents tranquility and peace. The two young men wading out into the water represent the First Nations people reaching out to help their people. The salmon represent the First Nations people struggling to survive.

Historical context
The story may have originated before the contact with early European explorers and traders. The Tsimshian people have an oral tradition of more than 20,000 years. Details
This story is one of several given to us by the Kwakiutl people to explain the origins of their village. It is a variation on the theme of the man stranded at a feast, a common motif in the folklore of many native North American tribes. In this version, the hero is not the man stranded at the feast, but the two young men who rescue him. The story provides an explanation for the presence of gold in the Kwakiutl territory, and also reinforces the idea that hospitality to strangers can be rewarding.

This is a good place to be when it's foggy and calm."  They argued about it, but neither was convinced by the other. Suddenly, a noise closer than before caught their attention. They looked around and saw a group of Native Americans coming towards them. The Native Americans told the two young men that a great storm was coming and that they should go back to their homes. The two young men did not want to disobey the Native Americans, but they were afraid of the storm. They decided to go back to Egulac as fast as they could. But just as they were about to turn the corner to go back home, they saw a group of Native Americans being swept away by the water. The two young men were terrified and turned around to go back to the Native Americans to help them, but they had vanished. The two young men were stranded on the beach, with nowhere to go. They huddled together for warmth, waiting for the storm to pass. After a while, the fog lifted and the two young men saw a light in the distance. They followed it until they came to a village. The villagers took them in and fed them. The two young men were overjoyed to be safe and began a new life in the village.

This story is from the Tlingit people. Does this story have a moral or message?
Yes, the story has a few moral messages. One message is that listening to advice from others can help us avoid danger. Another message is that disobeying authority or rules can lead to trouble. A third message is that listening to our surroundings and obeying our instincts can help us survive. Finally, a fourth message is that when we help others, we can make a difference in their lives and our own.

They heard a strange noise. One of them said: "Let's make it go away." So they made a racket, shouting and banging pots and pans, and the noise went away. They were happy and proud of themselves, thinking they had made the fog go away. But really it was just a normal occurrence that cleared up on its own. They got ice from the river to take home and went back to Egulac. On the way they talked about what had happened and began to feel foolish. So they decided to keep their eyes open and ears open, and to be careful about what they did, so as not to offend the fog.

Variant: one version has it that the two young men were out on the sea in a canoe and heard a strange noise which they thought was a whale. Thinking quickly they lit a fire on the beach which they believed would hide the light from the whale and so avoid being swallowed.

Interpretation
This tale is one of several from the Kwaw-Konani stories of the Tlingit people. It is a common theme in Indigenous American literature that the world was created in a foggy, chaotic time. In this story, the two young men are taken from the land of Egulac (a possible reference to Egloolit, a  Tlingit ancestral village near Yakutat) to Kwaw (a Tlingit village located near Sitka, Peruvanichikudeni (Peter Armstrong) and Kakasan (Frank Isaac) go to Kwaw to become sacred leaders, but they are also taken there to be protected from the dangerous fog.

Iktok was a supernatural being, and when the two men went to help him, they saw that he was trapped between two rocks. The two men decided that they did not want to live forever without the sun and the moon, and so they thanked Iktok and left. Iktok then decided to take one of them, Tleilxw, as his successor, and the two of them went off into the night.

This story is important because it shows the relationship between the people of the Northwest Coast and the spirit world. The people believed that there was a spirit world, populated by beings like Iktok, the Raven, who could help or hurt people as they saw fit. The people also believed that they could interact with this world, and that sometimes people were taken from the human world to the spirit world, as happened to Tleilxw.

The story is also frequently used in teaching Tlingit language and culture.

They heard a strange sound, like the sound of waves blowing through a narrow passage. They followed the sound until they came to a small beach, where they saw a strange sight. There were hundreds of thousands of stars in the sky, and the fog was so thick that it seemed to be raining stars.

The men realized that this was a strange and wonderful phenomenon that they had never seen before. They went back to their village and told everyone else about the stars, but no one believed them. The men had seen many strange things in their lives, but this was the strangest thing of all.

From that day on, the two young men went down to the river every night to watch the stars. They told stories about the constellations and the myths behind them, and the other villagers finally believed them. The men had discovered a wonderful natural wonder, and shared it with their community, bringing them all closer together.

In reality, the phenomenon is known as a noctilucent cloud. It occurs when tiny ice crystals form in the upper atmosphere and reflect the light from the moon and stars. They are most commonly seen in the arctic circles. While noctilucent clouds have been observed for hundreds of years, it was not until the 19th century that they were finally scientifically explained.

Afterward
The boy grew up and became a great hunter. He helped his friends and family by sharing his knowledge and skills. He married a girl from a nearby village and they had a son. The boy's name was Kwa, and he also became a great hunter. Kwa had a little brother who was very ill. Kwa and his father went to the medicine woman, but she couldn't help the boy. They took him to the forest and left him there, asking the forest to take him in. The forest took him in, and he grew up to become a powerful medicine man. He could heal people who were ill, no matter where they lived. He became famous throughout the whole northwest coast.

Unlikely friends
The story of Kuya and Pua is an important one in the mythology of the Tsimshian people. It tells how two young men from a rival tribe helped a native woman in need, and how their kindness was repaid many years later. In the tale, the two young men are from Egulac, which is located north of Metlakatla, where the story takes place. The Tsimshian people were fierce competitors for resource-rich territory, and battles between the tribes were common. Despite this, the story shows that even in the fiercest of rivalries, there was room for kindness and compassion.

Crescent Island
Crescent Island is a small island of 4.7 hectares (12 acres), with a circumference of 1600 metres (5200 ft), located 1 kilometre (1⁄2 nautical mile) off the northwest corner of Galiano Island in the Straight of Georgia. It is covered with thick vegetation and has a rocky shoreline. The island is privately owned and not open to the public.
Crescent Island is famous for its rare and exotic plant life. It has its own unique ecosystem with its own version of the typical Pacific Northwest rainforest. The island is so thickly covered with trees and vegetation that it is virtually unknown to most people. Only a handful of people have seen it.
The island is completely surrounded by a ring of rocks. Long ago, before the trees grew so dense, the natives used to come and hunt on the island. They used to hunt seals, hence the name. Nowadays, the only people who come are scientists and botanists.

The Egulac Seawolf
The Egulac Seawolf was a large war canoe or canadore that was built around 1860 by the Tsimshian people at Egulac, on the north coast of British Columbia. It was 110 feet (34 m) long, and 16 feet (4.9 m) wide. It had a draft of 3 feet (0.91 m) and drew 8 feet (2.4 m) of water. It weighed 10,900 pounds (4,900 kg) when fully equipped.
The Seawolf was armed with six 30-pound (14 kg) cannon, and carried a crew of 80 paddlers. It was said to be the most fearsome weapon in the Tsimshian arsenal.

Discovery and destruction
The Seawolf was discovered in 1870 by a party of Surveyors from the Province of British Columbia. They heard a strange cry. It was almost like a bird, but they didn't know what it was. They went to bed that night not worrying about it.
The next day they went out in the fog to hunt seals again. They heard the cry again, and this time they saw a strange bird flying away. It was white and had six feet, and although they didn't catch it that day, they were determined to find out what it was.
They went to the wise old man of the village and told him what they has seen. He told them that the creature was called the "Spirit Bear", and that it was very rare. He warned them never to go out in the fog again, because the Spirit Bear could not be defeated.
The two young men did not heed the old man's warning. They went out in the fog again, and once more they heard the cry of the Spirit Bear. Suddenly, out of the fog, came a huge white bear with six feet, just as the old man had described. The two young men were afraid, and they turned to run. But the bear was too fast. It caught one of the young men and carried him away.
The other young man ran back to the village and told the old man what had happened. The old man was sad, because he had warned them to stay away from the Spirit Bear. The young man who had been taken was never seen again.

Tlingit people
The Tlingit people are one of the four major indigenous groups of Alaska, along with the Haida, Alutiiq, and Inuit. They originally lived in the Northeast Pacific coastal area of the Olympic Peninsula, along the coasts of Southeast Alaska, on the north Funnel Bend of the Panhandle, and along the inner coastal area of Prince William Sound. They are known for their woodcarving, which was an important part of their culture. Their population in 1990 was 9,200.

Culture
The Tlingit people were a maritime culture, and their history is closely intertwined with the natural environment. Their mythology revolves around the transformations of animals into human beings, and the trickster figure Raven, who is the culture hero of the Tlingit people. Raven is usually portrayed as a black crow, but sometimes he is depicted as a human being. In some stories, Raven is a culture hero who brought fire to the people. In other stories, he is a trickster who gets into trouble because he is lazy or because he is jealous of other animals.

The people of Egulac had a rule: whoever saved a life, whether it belonged to a woman or a man, was allowed to live in the village forever. The two young men had saved a life each, but they were never found. They had disappeared.

This story is from the Tlingit people.

They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "Let's go home, this is not a good place to be when it's foggy and calm." The other said, "Let's stay here, this is a good place to be when it's foggy and calm." You might think that the first statement is true, but the second is not.  In fact, both statements are true.  The difference between them is a matter of perspective.  The first speaker is thinking about going home to Egulac, whereas the second speaker has a broader perspective and is thinking about going home to the village of Kimmik.  From Kimmik, it is true that it is a good place to be when it's foggy and calm, because the river is calm and the fog allows them to catch seals that are usually hard to see.  But from Egulac, it is not a good place to be, because the fog makes it hard to find the way home.  This is an example of how different perspectives can change the meaning of a statement.

The police were surprised to find two white men among the attackers. It was determined that the three men had been robbers terrorizing the area. Possible dates
The incident occurred sometime between 1895 and 1912, according to Charles L. Campana, a researcher who has compiled data from newspapers and other sources.  The exact date is unknown.

Names of the people involved
The names of the two young men from Egulac are not known.  The names of the three robbers are not known either.  The Indian who cried for help was probably from the Ksan group, the only group in the area at the time.  According to researcher Campana, the Indian was probably named Kasun, but that name may have been a alias.  The police report does not mention a name for the Indian.

Location of the robbery
The robbery took place near the confluence of the Ksan River and the Skeena River, about 10 miles (16 km) south of where the two rivers join.  The location is now known as Robber's Cove.

After the incident
After the incident, the two white men were taken to jail in Telegraph Creek.  They were later tried and convicted of robbery and assault.  One of the men was sentenced to five years in jail.  The other was sentenced to seven years in jail.  After serving their sentences, they returned to Victoria and made a living as detectives.

Tiramis
Tiramis is the sea spirit of the Strait of Egulac, a narrow stretch of water between Cape Luz and the mainland, in the Pacific Northwest.  She is sometimes called the Sea Wolf, and is reputed to have black fur and bright eyes.  She lives in a rocky cave, and spends most of her life under water, only coming to the surface to breathe.  Although she is a spirit, Tiramis is also considered a guardian of the sea, protecting sailors and fishermen from the treacherous currents and fogs of the strait.  Her spirit is sometimes invoked by sailors, who leave offerings of tobacco and salmon at her cave, hoping for her protection.

Prehistory
The story of Tiramis is known from several oral traditions of the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. Both stories involve the spirit being released from captivity and returning to the sea.

This story is from the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest coast of North America. It is a story that explains the origin of the fog on the coast. There are many variations of this story, but the essential elements are always the same: a test of worthiness by the spirits of the water, and the lifting of the fog to reveal a ghostly canoe. This story is often told as a part of the Tlingit creation story, in which the world was created by the actions of a powerful trickster.

Analysis
This story is from the Tlingit people of the northern Coast of British Columbia, Canada. The story is a good example of the Tlingit people's relationship with the environment. In the story, the hunters are out on the water hunting seals, which is a common Tlingit activity, but the fog that comes in is also a common occurrence in the Tlingit homeland, and one that is accurately represented in their stories. The sounds in the story are also important, as the Tlingit people have a rich tradition of oral storytelling, but also because sounds are so important in the Tlingit environment, with many creatures relying on sound for communication.

This story is from the Tlingit people, who tell it as a warning about the consequences of careless speech. According to one version of the story, the two hunters were brothers who had always obeyed their father by making sure they clearly stated their purpose whenever they went out hunting. But on this occasion, one of them – eager to add a “strange” element to the story – neglected to do so, with disastrous consequences.

Variations
There are several variations of this story, some of which have the two hunters arguing over which of them should go first, with one of them saying, "I'll go first, and if anything happens to me, you'll know it was because of me." In another version, the two hunters are not brothers but close friends who make a solemn promise to each other that they will always go hunting together. They agree that if one of them dies, the other will make sure he is properly buried. But when one of them is killed by a giant beaver, the survivor is so overcome by grief that he is unable to carry out the promise, and as a result, the dead hunter's ghost comes back to haunt him.

The Tlingit people were some of the first inhabitants of the area that is now known as British Columbia. They are one of the three major cultural groups that make up the Tsimshian people, along with the Kwakiutl and Haida, who were also indigenous to the area. The Tlingit people are now concentrated in a few areas along the northern and inner coasts of British Columbia, as well as in Alaska.

The Tlingit people were skilled hunters, fishers, and traders. They lived in small, tight-knit communities, and were self-sufficient in food. Each community was independent, and there was little centralized authority among the Tlingit. This changed when contact with Europeans began.

They heard a strange sound, something like someone crying. They followed the sound and came upon a sight that turned their blood to ice. It was a sight that none of them would ever forget as long as they lived.

This is the story of Egulac, a traditional Ojibway ghost story from the Algonquian tribe of North America. It is reported that the original story is over 300 years old and has been passed down through the generations by word of mouth.

The story
The story begins with two young men from Egulac, a village on the north shore of Lake Superior, who went out onto the lake to hunt seals. It was late in the year and the two men had decided that it was time to store their hunting gear for the winter. They had caught a few seals earlier in the year but nothing to write home about. This particular night was foggy and calm, the kind of night that makes sailors uneasy. As they were about to turn back, they heard a strange sound, a sound like someone was crying.
They followed the sound until they came upon a sight that turned their blood to ice. There, on the shore, was a woman whose body was all white, like the snow that falls from the sky in winter. But her eyes were red as blood.
The two men were terrified. They turned to run, but the woman beckoned to them, staring at them with those red eyes. She spoke to them, but they could not understand her. She pointed to the water and made a motion with her arms. Then she vanished into the mist.
The two men were left standing there, alone and confused. They had seen something that defied explanation. Was it a dream? A trick of the mind? They did not know, but they knew one thing for certain. They would tell no one of what they had seen.

Variants
One version has the two hunters going out in a canoe and hearing the foghorn of a passing ship, which they take to be the sound of the river ice breaking up. When they go to investigate, they see a seal lying on the ice, and as they approach it, it crashes through the ice and swims away. They follow it to the edge of the fogbank, where it disappears.
Another version has the two hunters out on the sea in a canoe when they hear the sound of a seal's head breaking up, and they grab their harpoons and start after it. But as they approach the place where the sound came from, they see that it was only a piece of ice that had broken off from the glacier, and the sound was just the running water.

One variant has it that the woman was not on the river bank but in the water itself, and that the two men fished her out and tried to help her, only to have her sink back into the water and sing the same haunting melody.

This story is found among the Kwakiutl and among the Dene. It is also found among the Inupiat with the title "The Woman of Immortality".

They heard a strange sound, different from anything they had heard before. It was an echo of a cry of a young girl, lost and alone.

The story
The story is that of a young girl who lived with her father, the chief, at Egulac, near the mouth of the Columbia River. She was alone when she cried out, lost and afraid, and the two young men heard her cries as an echo. They went in search of the girl, but as they approached the place where she lived, the fog grew thicker and thicker until they could go no farther. They returned to the village and told everyone they had heard a cry of a lost girl, and a search party was organized. Many of the villagers went out, but they too became lost in the fog, and soon it grew dark. Everyone made their way back to the village, frightened and anxious.
The girl was never found.

Variants
There are variations to this story, usually involving a boy instead of a girl, but the essential elements remain the same. In one version, the boy is out hunting ducks when he hears the cry. In another, the boy hears the cry of his sister, who has gone out to gather firewood.

Story origin

They tell stories about how the masters of law created the world and the rules that they made for people to live by. This story is one of the many tales that tell of the great flood that covered the world in water.

Description
This is a story from the Tlingit people of a battle between humans and a sea monster. The monster was so large that it required four canoes to carry its carcass. The monster had lived in the water near Egulac for a very long time and nobody had seen it before. The monster was pulled to land and a feast was held in its honour. After everyone had eaten, the leftovers were buried near the river. Later, two young men went to the river to hunt seals and heard the unusual noise. They investigated and found the buried remains of the sea monster. The monster had a neck that was twice the length of a normal sea monster's neck. It was so large that it took many people to carry its carcass. The people decided to bury it again, but this time they built a large mound over its burial place. On the mound they placed four large stones, which represented the four canoes that had pulled the monster to land. They also placed a large flat rock near the base of the mound. This rock was said to have been the head of the sea monster. The people celebrated for four days and then went back to their homes.

Historical context
This story is about the shipwreck of the SS Beaverton that ran aground on Egulac Island in Kentucky on October 26, 1918. The vessel was a Canadian ship carrying war materials to the Allies during World War I. The shipwreck is remembered locally as one of the greatest disasters to have befallen the residents of the region.

Folklore
The story of the SS Beaverton is part of the folklore of the inland waterways of Kentucky. Variants of the story are told about other shipwrecks on other rivers in the Midwest. In all versions, the heroic actions of two young men save the day. In some versions, the men are brothers. In others, they are not. But in all versions, the villagers are reluctant to get involved, for various reasons: fear of the unknown, fear of the water, or fear of the authorities. Only the bravery of these two young men, often identified as Native Americans, saves the day.

This is a story from the Tlingit people, who live (and first lived) near the northwest coast of British Columbia, Canada. It was a still, calm night, and as they sat there, the fog came in and covered everything. Suddenly, they heard a noise. It was a woman screaming. One of the young men said, "I think we should go and see what's wrong." The other said, "No, let's pretend we're asleep." But as they lay there, they heard more noises, and eventually, they decided to go and see what had happened. When they got to the woman's house, they saw that she was indeed in trouble – she was giving birth. The two young men helped her, and when it was over, the mother thanked them. From that day on, the two young men were known as the brave ones who had helped a woman in need, and they were held in high esteem by everyone in the village.

The very next day, a massive earthquake struck, and a large tsunami followed. The earthquake was so great that it was felt as far as New York. The damage was tremendous, whole islands were destroyed, and countless numbers of people died. It was one of the worst natural disasters in recorded history.
The two young men who had heard the singing were the only ones who survived the tsunami. They spent the rest of their lives trying to find the source of the singing, in hopes of preventing another disaster. They traveled to the most remote parts of the north, braving the harshest weather conditions, and living off the land.
They say that to this day, you can hear the songs of the north wind, if you listen closely. And if you're lucky, you might just catch a glimpse of the two young men, still on their eternal quest.

They heard a strange noise, and then saw a light coming towards them. It was the light of an oncoming train. The men had gone to the wrong place and were now stranded on the railway tracks leading to the Hyeasun.

History
The Hyeasun railway line was built in 1877 by the Canadian Pacific Railway company. It was built for the purpose of transporting cargo to and from the ships that docked at the port of Victoria, British Columbia. The line was originally planned to continue south towards the US border, but bad negotiations with the United States government resulted in the termination of the line in Victoria.

Stranding
The two men were stranded on the tracks for nearly two days before a train came along and saw them. It was the westbound CPR train bound for Vancouver. The train stopped and the conductor helped the two men on board. The train then continued on its way to Vancouver.

Afterwards
After they arrived in Vancouver, the two men went to the police and reported what had happened. The police were skeptical of their story, as it was unusual for fog to be so thick on the inner harbour. The men were told to go home and not to worry about it. But the police eventually believed them and began an investigation.
Further investigations revealed that the fog had been caused by a chemical spill at the water treatment plant. The fog was so thick that it had disoriented the men, causing them to wander onto the train tracks.

Conclusion
The two men were lucky to have survived. They had gone hunting for seals, but ended up on the wrong path. It was a lesson in paying attention to the warnings issued by Transport Canada. The men could have easily have been killed or seriously injured. As it was, they were just shaken up. They never forgot that lesson, and from then on, they always double-checked their destinations before setting out.

The breaking dam
In 1873, a 3200 ft long dam was built across the southern arm of the Fraser River to collect water for the Kootenay and Rocky Mountain Trench Railways.  The dam was made by piling up large rocks, with a 16 ft high wall made of wood piles and surrounded by 14 ft high earthen embankments.  There was a 15 ft wide channel on the upstream side of the dam for the water to flow through.  On October 20, 1874, with the thunder of approaching rain clouds, two hundred men worked frantically to complete the dam.  The last stone was placed at 11:30 pm.  Shortly after midnight the rain started, and the temperature dropped.  The river ice began to crack and by 4:00 am the dam was leaking.  By 7:00 am the leak was 100 ft long and the water was flowing over the top of the dam.  The crew worked frantically to repair the dam, but the water was too deep and the stones too slippery.  Eventually, 12 miles of the railway track was submerged and the damage was estimated at $2 million.  The crew was able to stop the water by building a 900 ft long dike across the mouth of the Fraser.  Although the dam was repaired in 1875, it was never put into operation.  The railway was built along the north arm of the Fraser River.

They heard a strange noise, and one of them said it was the sound of the sea crying.  Their frightened voices echoed in the fog, and they made their way back to Egulac as fast as they could.

They told everyone they heard the sea crying and the next day a group of men went to the river to search for the source of the noise.  They couldn't find anything, but as the fog lifted they saw a great number of calm, clear pools of water where there had been rough, turbid waters before.  It was said that from that day on the people of Egulac were careful what they did, so that the sea would not cry again.

Variants

They followed the sound until they came to a large pool of water.  On the edge of the pool they saw the reflection of a face, but when they approached the water to get a closer look, the face disappeared and the water became smooth and still, as if nothing had happened.

Another variant has it that the two young men were out on the sea in a canoe when they heard a woman's voice calling for help.  They looked around but could not see anyone.  Then they saw a light in the distance and followed it to the pool of water where they found a woman lying on the shore, almost dead from exposure.  They carried her to the village and took care of her, and from that day on the people of the village treated her kindly.

The Niobes were a prehistoric people who lived along the northwest coast of Canada in what is now known as the Kitimat area during the late stages of the last glacial period. The men were amazed by the sight and decided to hide and watch. They saw that the Niobes had a large feast, with many animals being eaten. The men were very curious and wanted to know more about the people. So they decided to approach the village and make contact.

The men realized that these people must be the ones who had painted the rocks they had seen earlier. They felt a little scared, but they were curious and wanted to know more.

The young men then cut open Nattil's body and removed his heart. They then put the heart into a canoe and set it adrift on the river. Later, when they returned to Egulac, they found that a great feast had been prepared. They ate and danced all night, but nobody would tell them what had happened to Nattil's body. In the morning, they went to the river to continue searching for seals, but instead they went out in the canoe and found Nattil's body tucked safely in a tree. They were relieved to have him back and took him to the village for burial.
After Nattil's funeral, the people of Egulac decided to move to a new village site further up the river. The old village was abandoned, and the people went down to the river to burn the old buildings. While they were there, they noticed a beaver on the river bank. One of the men went over to kill it, but as he was raising his weapon, the beaver talking to him, saying that he was really a man who had been turned into a beaver by the trickster, Coyote. The man was startled by this, and Coyote appeared out of nowhere and grabbed him. He was taken to the beaver's lodge, where he was transformed back into a man. From then on, the people lived in harmony with the animals, and there was plenty of food and wealth in the village.
