They heard a strange sound, and then they saw a light coming towards them. It was a ghost ship.
The men were afraid and tried to get back to the safety of the shore, but the ghost ship followed them. They saw that the ship had no sails or oars, and it just floated along, making a ghostly moaning sound.
The men tried to avoid the ship, but then they saw that there were other ghost ships all around them, surrounded by a fog that hid the land. They were trapped!
Just then, another ship appeared through the fog. It was a ship of ghosts. The two men were afraid, but the ghost ship's crew came over and calmed them. They explained that they were the ferrymen of the dead, and that they had come to take the men across the river of death.
The men got onto the ghost ship and it set sail for the land of the dead. They saw strange things on the way, like rivers of fire and mountains of gold, but they were afraid and just wanted to leave that place.
When they reached the land of the dead, they saw that it was just like the world of the living, only more beautiful. Here, the two men could choose any path they wanted to follow. They decided to follow the path of the righteous, and so they lived happily in the land of the dead.
But there was one thing they wondered about: the two ghost ships that had followed them to the land of the dead. Where had they come from, and how had they been built?
The answers to these questions would remain a mystery, because the story of the two young men from Egulac is just a story, a tale told long ago to scare people into behaving themselves. And even though we may never know the answers to these questions, one thing is certain: the ghost ships of the Takarunai are always there, waiting for the ferrymen of the dead to claim another soul.

Word origin
Egulac, a village on the northwest shore of Lake Superior in Michilimakina.  The word comes from an Ojibwe phrase meaning "where the ground freezes early"  (Lake Superior freezes early and often.)  The early freezing ground is useful for both farming and harvesting nuts and berries.  The village is now part of the town of Grand Portage, Minnesota.

Tlingit culture
The Tlingit people are one of the three main groups of Native Americans who live in Alaska. The other two are the Haida and the Kwakiutl. The Tlingit originated in the Southeast Alaska region hundreds of years ago. They were a powerful group who controlled the trade in furs between Russia, Canada, and the United States. The Tlingit are known for their beautiful artwork, which includes carvings, mask, and totem poles. Tlingit art is highly collectible and is often seen in museums and private collections around the world.

The Tlingit people are one of the many Native American tribes that have a rich storytelling tradition. Tlingit stories are passed down from generation to generation, and they help to explain the world around them. These stories can be found in the book "Tlingit Stories" edited by Ernestine Kayes and published by Seal Press in 1997.

Context
The story of the Guardian of the River can be found in the section of the book called "Stories from the Upper World". This section of the book tells stories that "describe the creation of the world, the way things really are, and the way they should be". The story of the Guardian of the River is a warning story, a story that tells people what will happen if they don't follow the proper way of doing things.

Characteristics
Tlingit stories are known for their rich use of imagery and symbolism. They often feature animals and supernatural beings that have special meanings. The stories are also known for their flexibility. A single story can be told in many different ways, with each teller adding their own insights and interpretations. The stories are not just told, they are performed. Tellers use voice, body language, and props

They heard a strange noise. One of them said, "That's the sound of the sea level rising." They knew that if the tide came in, they would be cut off from the mainland and soon be swept away. They started to run up the hill towards Egulac, calling warning signals as they went. They shouted, "Come quickly, the tide is coming in!" But no one came. Everyone in the village thought it was just a warning signal for a night of heavy rain, and nobody went out. Only one old man and his grandson, who lived in a cabin at the edge of the marsh, came out to help. They watched as the two young men, exhausted from running, fell into a deep sleep on the hillside. The old man and his grandson waited and watched as the tide came in, sweeping away the village of Egulac.

Variants
In some versions of the story, the two young men are not from Egulac but from a different village, and they go to warn Egulac. In one version, told by Tlicho Dene elder Murray Pepper, the villagers don't believe the warning because it is out of season for tidal waves. In a version told by Adam Fortunate Snow, the villagers don't believe the warning because the young man who gives it is known for telling tales.

Origin
It is not known where the story originated. It is told among the Tutchone people and among the Athna people of the Athna First Nation.

They heard a strange noise, which they had never heard before, and it was coming from the stream. They huddled together and listened. It was a sound like running water, but it was coming from the woodland. They investigated and found a hidden den, where they discovered a monster about twelve feet long, with a head like a frog, and eyes that glowed in the dark. The men were afraid and tried to leave, but the monster came out and blocked their way. It made a gesture with its hand, and in a moment a group of strangers appeared. They were friendly and told the men that the monster was their king. The men bowed and asked for his permission to hunt seals. The king granted them permission, but warned them that if they hurt any seal, even accidentally, they would be lost. The men agreed and went away. After a while, the two friends returned to the river, and as they approached the spot where they had seen the king, the fog grew thicker and thicker, until it was so thick that they could no longer see each other. One of the men called out, "What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: ?" and the other replied, "I can't see you either." Soon afterward, a great storm arose, and the two friends died. The king had kept his word, and they had been lost.

They heard a strange sound, different from anything they had heard before. They didn’t know what it was, but they decided it was a good omen and they called it the 'Egulac sound'. They returned to their camp and told everyone else about the sound and from then on, whenever they went out on the water, they listened for the Egulac sound. They believed that if they heard it, everything would go well. But one night, as they paddled out to the hunting grounds, they heard a loud crack, and a big wave swept over them. It was an earthquake! The ground shook and there was chaos everywhere. The men in the canoes were separated and there was no Egulac sound to guide them. Some of the men drowned, but two of them managed to swim to shore and they made it back to the village just as the sun was rising. They were tired and cold, but they were grateful to be alive. From then on, the hunting parties never went out in the fog, no matter how calm it seemed. And they never heard the Egulac sound again. But the men of Egulac never forgot the lessons they had learned that night. They knew that the sound they had heard was just a trick of the wind, but the earthquake had been a reminder that nature could be unpredictable and dangerous, even on the calmest of nights.

This story is from the Tlingit people, who live in the northwest of British Columbia, Canada. It is a reminder that nature is unpredictable and can be dangerous, even on the calmest of nights.

The River Spirit
The Egulac men were intrigued and asked the River Spirit many questions. It told them that long ago, in the time before the first people came, it had taken on a human shape and lived among them. It had taught them many things, but they had turned against it, and so it had retreated into the river. It still watched over them, but no longer interfered in their affairs.

The canoe
One of the young men asked the River Spirit how it was that they had never seen it before, despite its claims to have lived among their ancestors. The River Spirit explained that it had taken the form of a canoe, but that the people had forgotten its true nature. "You have forgotten how to see me," it said. "Look again."

The journey
The River Spirit offered to take them on a journey, a spirit journey, to show them wonders they had never seen before. The two young men climbed into the canoe and it set off, leaving the foggy river behind. For days they travelled, seeing incredible things. They went to the upside-down world, where rivers flowed upward and trees grew to great heights. They saw creatures they had never imagined, strange birds with heads but no bodies, and fish that were the colour of the sky.

But as they journeyed, the two young men began to forget. They started to argue about trivial things, and soon they were fighting each other. The River Spirit watched as the two fighters stumbled and fell into the water. "You have forgotten how to see me," it said again. "Look again."

In fact, the noise was caused by the wind, which had suddenly gusted across the calm water. The men had simply misinterpreted the sound, a common occurrence in unfamiliar environments.

They heard a strange noise, and one of them said to the other: "Let us go home; this is not a good place to be when it is foggy and calm." But the other replied: "There is no hurry; let us just watch what happens." Soon a third person came along and said: "Let us go home; this is not a good place to be when it is foggy and calm."  This continued until nine people had arrived. By that time, the fog had lifted and it was no longer calm. The ten people decided to go home, but as they were crossing the river, they fell into the water and were drowned.

Analysis
This is a story from the Chinook word picture tradition, a body of oral and written narrative that was popular among the Chinook and other Native American tribes of the Pacific Northwest. The story is a cautionary tale, warning people not to go out into the foggy and calm river when they cannot see what is happening around them. The tale may have been used to explain freak accidents that occurred when people drowned in the river under similar circumstances.

Patsy's Lament
In the early days, before the white man came,
There was peace in Egulac, peace in Wenatchee,
But now it is gone,
Gone like the salmon that once filled the rivers.

My father, Klahanie, was the greatest chief,
Of all the Cree, he was the bravest warrior,
But now he is gone, dead and buried.
I cry for him, I mourn for him,
As I cry and mourn for all that we have lost.

The white man came with violence and hate,
They took our land, they took our freedom,
They killed our people, they killed my father.
I hear their guns, I see their horses,
I hate them, I will never be their slave.

But now I am alone, I am weak,
I hear the wolves, I fear the cold,
I cry for my father, I cry for myself,
For the future is dark, it is hopeless.

The two young men listened to her story, and then they did something that would change things forever. They took her back to Egulac, and presented her to the tribe as the Daughter of Klahanie. And from that day on, Patsy became a leader of the Cree people, a woman of great power and influence. She was the one who led the resistance against the white men, and she became a legend in her own right. She was Patsy, the Warrior Woman.

Explanation
This is a story from the Tlingit people, told by Keith Smith to Victoria Holspice in 1968. It is a cautionary tale, warning of the dangers of staying out on the river when it is foggy and calm, and of the importance of being able to run away quickly if necessary. The story also implies that there are supernatural enemies who can come out of the ground, and that they are to be avoided at all costs. Overall, the story can be seen as reinforcing the idea that nature should be respected and that humans are not the masters of the natural world, but are subject to its forces and require a humility towards the environment.

This is a Native American story from the Tlingit people. It is important to recognize that in many indigenous languages, including Tlingit, the concepts of "animal," "monster," and "spirit" are not distinct categories. In Tlingit, for instance, a spirit can take on the form of an animal or a human, and an animal can be possessed by a spirit. In this story, the monster is obviously not a natural part of the environment, but is rather a supernatural being. This being is clearly harmful, but it is also clear that it is trying to warn the people of Egulac about something. Like all Tlingit stories, this story must be read with an awareness of the cultural and historical context in which it was told.

They had both been standing up in the canoe at the time of the confusion. This type of fog is called a radiant fog, where the sun is on the horizon and refracts the light rays, making the fog glow. It is also known as a white fog or frost fog.

The story is from the Tlingit people of the southeast Alaskan coast.

They heard a strange screaming sound which seemed to be coming from the water. Then they saw a dark shape moving on the water. It was a seal, but it was unlike any seal they had ever seen. This was no ordinary seal; it was a seal monster.
The men lived through the night and told the tale of the seal monster to the Egulac people. From that day on the Egulac people kept a watchful eye on the sea and nobody went out hunting seals anymore.

Possible causes of the story
There are several possible causes for the origin of the story of the seal monster:

A natural phenomenon
The foggy night with a strange screaming sound and a dark shape moving on the water could have been caused by a natural phenomenon such as a shoal of fish or an underwater landslide.

A legend to explain an accident
The story of the seal monster could be a legend which explains an accident which happened to someone from Egulac while they were hunting seals. Maybe someone drowned or was swept out to sea and the story of the seal monster was created to hide the true cause of the accident.

A warning
The story of the seal monster could be a warning not to go out hunting seals anymore. The penalty for ignoring the warning could be death.

A wish-fulfillment story
The story of the seal monster could be a wish-fulfillment story. It could be a story about someone who caught a very big seal and became rich and famous.

A story to explain a cultural practice
The story of the seal monster could be a story which explains a cultural practice among the Egulac people. Maybe the people of Egulac used to hunt seals for food and the story was created to explain why they no longer do this.

The story of the two young men from Egulac is a warning story. It tells us that the tide is unpredictable and can turn quickly. The two young men decided to follow the sound, and as they walked along the shoreline, the fog lifted and they could see a small island nestled just off the main shore.  The island was covered in snow, and it seemed to be glowing with an inner light.

The men stood there, transfixed, as a group of white birds came flying out of the sky and landed on the island.  The birds were like nothing the men had ever seen before, and they seemed to radiate light as they sang a hauntingly beautiful song.  The men were awestruck by the sight, and they knew that they were witnessing something truly magical.

Suddenly, the fog rolled in again, and the men were unable to see where the island had gone.  They turned to leave, but as they walked back towards the main shore, they could hear the sound of the birdsong echoing in their ears, a beautiful memory of the magical night they had witnessed.

From that day on, the two young men made a point to visit the island whenever they went out hunting.  They knew that the island was a special place, a place where the beauty of nature could be appreciated in all its glory.  And they were not mistaken – the island had a profound effect on the men, and they went on to live long, happy lives, filled with love and wonder.  And they knew that the magic of the island had been a part of that happiness.

So if you ever find yourself feeling lost or lonely, remember the tale of the two young men from Egulac, and make your way to the island of dreams, where the beauty of nature will fill your heart and your soul.

The island of Tumtum
The island that the two young men found was called Tumtum by the natives. It lived up to its name; it was a strange and weird place. The men soon discovered that the island was inhabited by spirits. A strange court

A strange request
Before they left the island, the two men made a strange request. They asked the spirits to make them stupid, so that they would be no use to their competitors back in Egulac. The spirits granted their request.

Back in Egulac

They had become stupid and useless to their competitors.

They put them in a box and took them to the "Seal Doctor" in Victoria. But before they did that, they went to see their friend, the famous marine biologist Dr. John Cunningham. He lived in a small house on Lulu Island, and when he answered the door, he saw the two baby seals in the box and said, "These are sister and brother. Let me take care of them." And he did. Soon it was time for the baby seals to go back into the wild, but first they taught the children at the Centre how to hunt for their own food, and how to identify healthy seals vs. sick seals. They heard a voice crying for help. They went to investigate and found a woman in the water, near where the Egulac River joins the Fraser River. The woman was swept away by the current before they could reach her.
The young men went back to Egulac and told the news to the Egulac people. They went back to the place where the woman had been lost and found her body shortly later. They brought her body back to Egulac and held a potlatch to pay for the burial. They paid the family of the woman 100 sheets of silver and 100 blankets. After the potlatch the mood changed and people started to laugh. They realized that the woman was not really dead, but had played a trick on them.

Interpretation
This tale is one of several recorded by Frank Lindsay in the 1960s and 1970s that reflect the spiritual and social tensions emerging in the transition from potlatch to market economy in the Stó:lō and other First Nations. In this tale, the woman's body is both a symbol of the wealth transferred in the potlatch and a reminder of the deception and instability of the new economic order.

Although it is not clear where in the interior of British Columbia the story takes place, the "two young men from Egulac" were probably members of the Egulac Band of the Ktunaxa people.  The Ktunaxa originated in the inland area of the North Atlantic Ocean, between Alaska and British Columbia. The story is told in the Tłəla Qwala, a collection of Ktunaxa legends.In the legend of "The Two Young Men from Egulac," two young men went out in canoes to hunt seals on the sea. The calm, foggy night turned sour when the men's canoes were overturned, and they drowned. The bodies of the two young men were later found in a dream by a member of the Egulac Band. It is said that the two young men had been mistakenly killed by the Tlatlas, a rival group.  The Tlatlas were always an enemy of the Egulac, and frequently attacked their camps.After the young men were found, the Egulac people decided to move their camp to a new location, as the old place was bad luck.  They left the bodies of the two young men in the old camp, as they were unable to bury them. However, before they left, the Egulac people placed a rock on the grave of the two young men. According to the legend, the two rocks are visible on the side of the canoe that was used by the two young men. The rocks are said to be a reminder of the two young men who lost their lives while out hunting seals.

Geography
Orca Sound Tsimshian is a narrow, tidal, steep-sided channel with fast-moving tidal water moving through it. It connects Lakes Egulac and Chetwick, which are separated from the Pacific Ocean by a sand spit. The channel is about 1.5 kilometres (0.93 mi) long and 300 metres (980 ft) wide. It is guarded by a sand spit on the south side and by a rocky headland on the north side. The spit is an important landfall for ships and boats and was originally marked by a lightstation, which was removed in 1907 when a range beacon was established.
The channel is not without danger. In 1853, the steamship "Patrice O'Hara" ran ashore in the fog near theegulac Bar.  In 1905, the "City of Glasgow" grounded on the rocky headland at the north end of the sound. And in 1946, the "Southern Prince" struck the sand spit, causing the tug "Alberni" to run aground trying to assist.

Treaty of Egulac
The Egulac treaty was one of the most important treaties made by the fur trade companies with the Native peoples of the west coast of Canada. It was signed on August 18, 1851, by John McLean, on behalf of the Vancouver's Corporation, and by a group of Native chiefs, including Quwat, the chief of Egulac.

Trading company
The Hudson's Bay Company (HBC) and the North West Trading Company (NWTC) were the two major trading companies that traded with the Native people along the west coast of Canada. The HBC had been trading with the Native people since the early 18th century. The NWTC was a relatively new company when compared to the HBC. It was formed in 1827 with the blessing of the Hudson's Bay Company and with the intent of competing with the HBC for the trade of the Pacific Northwest.
The trading companies were the major forces in the development of the fur trade on the west coast of Canada. They financed the expeditions of the major explorers of the region, such as Lewis and Clark, as well as later expeditions. The expeditions were an integral part of the company's plan to expand the fur trade. The HBC and NWTC merged in 1859.

Interpretation
The story is a metaphor for the destructive power of nature, and the unpredictability of the natural environment. The two young men represent the overconfident hunters who underestimate the power of the sea and pay the price for their overconfidence. The story is also a warning to sailors to be wary of fog and rapid currents, which can hide hidden shallows and submerged obstacles.

Variants
A version of the story is found in the Tlingit collection of stories, where the two hunters are more specifically identified as being from the village of Tlake. The story is also found among the Kwakiutl, where it is related that the two hunters were brothers. The island tribe were very friendly and helped the villagers with their work. But one day, while they were out hunting, a great storm came up and many of the hunters drowned. The two young men from Egulac led their people back to the mainland. They were never seen again. Some say they went back to Star Village to live with the people from the island. That is why, to this day, there are always two young men from Star Village who go out to the hunting grounds, no matter how foggy or stormy the weather may be.

The story of Egulac is a Native American tale from the Kutenai people of the southeastern Rocky Mountains. The story is told as a cautionary tale about the dangers of wanting more than one is allotted. In the tale, a great spirit named Egulac lived at the bottom of a deep lake. He had the power to grant the wishes of those who placed a box of matches under the moon on a special night. However, he would only grant one wish to each person. Two young men from Egulac went out onto the lake one night, with a box of matches in tow, but they asked for more than one wish. This angered the great spirit, and he transformed them into seals as a punishment.

Variants
There are several variants of the Egulac story. In one version, the two young men are punished for speaking disrespectfully to the great spirit. In another, they are turned into frogs for taking more than their fair share of fish from the lake.

Seals have allergies too. When a seal is allergic to something in the water, it will bubble and foam at the mouth and may have trouble swimming. Sometimes seals get allergic reactions from eating the wrong thing, like a jellyfish.

Seals are sometimes culled to protect the salmon. Seals eat a lot of salmon and if there are too many seals, there will be no salmon left for people to eat. Sometimes people catch salmon and keep the eggs so that there will be salmon to eat later.

Ecology
Seals live in the water all their life. They breathe air to live, but they spend most of their life underwater looking for food. They need to eat a lot of food to keep their energy up because they spend so much time swimming. In the spring and summer they eat fish and in the fall and winter they eat crabs and shrimp.

Endangered
Some species of seals are endangered. This means that they are in danger of disappearing forever. People want to help protect seals so that they will continue to exist. Some people hunt seals for their fur. This is not a sustainable practice because there are not enough seals to feed the demand for seal fur.

The story of the Canoe of Rogue is a folktale of the Tlingit people, and is often considered part of the Mukurtu story cycle. The tale is told in various versions, but the basic story is that two young men from Egulac (a village on the northern coast of Tlingit territory) went out in a canoe to hunt seals, and heard the voice of the Great Spirit (Teehaydi) speaking to them. The Spirit warned them that a great wave was coming, and that they must paddle faster than they had ever paddled before to reach the safety of the rocky shore. The two friends paddled as hard as they could, but the wave was so great that it swept the canoe away, and the two young men were lost.
Tlingit storyteller Howard I. Smith said that the story of the Canoe of Rogue was a cautionary tale, and that it should be told "to keep young people from going out in bad weather, especially in autumn, when the winds are unpredictable and sometimes fierce."

The tale of the Canoe of Rogue is often compared to the story of the Singing Sailor, which is also a warning about the dangers of going out to sea. In the Singing Sailor story, a coastal Tlingit family hears a sailor singing outside their house, but when they go to help him, they find that he has drowned.

The two young men agreed, and set off on a journey that would change their lives forever.

The journey
The journey to the island of Women took many years, and the two young men became respected members of the community. They hunted and fished and lived off the bounty of the land, and learned much from their fellow travellers. Some of the things they learned were how to make tools and weapons, how to plant and harvest crops, and how to live in harmony with the natural world. They also learned about the customs and traditions of the people who lived on the island, and gradually began to understand the real reason why the old man had brought them there.

The island of Women
The island of Women was a strange and wondrous place, populated by strange and wondrous creatures. There were birds with feathers the colour of the northern lights, and trees that grew apples as big as houses. The two young men explored the island, marveling at the sights they saw around them. They met women of all ages and descriptions, some beautiful and kind, some ugly and cruel. They learned that the women of this place were not like the women of the mainland. These women had the power to make or destroy civilizations, to bring riches or ruin, depending on the whims of their moods. The two young men soon discovered that they were to become slaves on this island, living at the mercy of these powerful women.

They heard a voice crying for help. They followed the sound and found a young woman being attacked by a group of men. She was buried there beneath the sand dunes near the river. The men were attempting to kill her because she was in love with a man they hated. The two young men fought off the attackers and saved the woman's life.
The next day the woman told them that she was really a selkie, a seal woman, and that the men who attacked her were from a rival tribe. She explained that sometimes selkies take human form and live among people, but that when they want to swim in the sea again, they must cast off their human skins and return to the water. She offered to repay their help by using her powerful voice to sing a song of protection for them.
The three of them lived happily ever after, spending their time in both human and seal form, and becoming known throughout the land as the singers of protection.

The moral of the story is that true love overcomes hatred and conflict, even in the face of physical violence. It also shows that there is power in the unity of two seemingly different groups, the humans and the selkies, who come together to form a stronger community.

They heard a voice calling them, and when they looked over their shoulder, they saw a light approaching them on the water. It was a canoe with three men in it, but when the light got closer, they could see that the three men were all one person with three heads. The three-headed monster dragged the canoe onto the shore and demanded that the two young men from Egulac give him their seals. The two men did so, and the three-headed monster then vanished with the seals, only to reappear further down the shore with two more heads. This process continued until he had a total of nine heads, at which point he disappeared completely into the fog, leaving the two young men stranded on the shore.

Variants
There are several variants of this story from different First Nations groups in Canada. In one version, the three-headed monster is not a malevolent force, but rather a manifestation of the three rivers that flow from the mountains. In another, the three heads represent the past, present, and future.

Symbolism
The three-headed monster represents the three rivers that flow from the mountains, but it also represents the three stages of life: birth, living, and death. The young men from Egulac represent all of humanity. The seals represent the dreams and goals that we have in life. The canoe represents the journey that we take through life. The fog represents the mysteries of the universe.

It was the light of a lamp, and as they drew nearer still the light grew brighter and brighter until they saw that it was a lamp in the window of a house. The light was so strong that it shone out into the foggy night like a beacon. The two young men went towards the door of the house and knocked. An old woman answered the door, and when she saw the two young men standing there in the fog, she screamed and cried out: "You two are going to marry my two children!". The two young men were startled by this statement, but they nodded and agreed to the old woman's request. The old woman then led them into the house and fed them a meal. After the meal she led them to two beds in a back room. One bed was for her youngest son, and the other was for her eldest son. The two young men went to sleep feeling very grateful for the hospitality they had received. In the morning when they awoke, the fog had lifted and the sun was shining brightly. The two young men went to the door of the house and looked out into the bright light of the sunny day. The old woman came to the door and said: "You may now take your leave, but you must promise me one thing." They agreed to anything she asked, and she said: "You must come back and visit me every year on the anniversary of this day." They promised to come back and visited her every year on the anniversary of that day for the rest of their lives.

Variations
There are numerous variations to this tale, with some versions featuring a group of three or four young men who all drown, while others feature a single hero who saves the elderly man only to drown himself. Some versions are set on a lake or a sound, rather than a river. In one variation, the old man is not actually rescued, but rather lures the young men to their deaths.

Origins
This story is told in a number of variations around the world. A common theme is the idea of getting into trouble on the water when the weather turns bad. This tale may have originated on the northwest coast of North America.

This is the story of the Eugnats, as told to Charles Wilkins by a Kwakiutl informant in 1884:

"Two young men went out to the beach intending to go out in a canoe to hunt seals. It was night and there was a fog, and as they were waiting for the canoe to be prepared a great earthquake happened, and they were both drowned."

This story is one of several tales that are told to explain earthquakes. Another common explanation is that an underwater volcano erupted and produced a great earthquake.

Similarly, in a tale from the South Pacific, told by the Raiatean people, an earthquake was caused when a great shark was trapped and crushed by a massive rock fell from the sky.

And in a story from the Gower Peninsula in Wales, told by the Llethyr people, an earthquake was caused when a great whirlpool swallowed a ship with all hands.

In some versions of the story, it is not Gasoo who is carried away by the current, but one of his sons. Origins
It is not known where the story of the night the world was saved originated. It is told in some versions as a separate tale, in others as part of the larger story of the Potato Famine. It has been collected from the Quatsa people, the Tlingit, and the Haida, among others.

The story of the night the world was saved can be seen as a cautionary tale about the dangers of ignoring warnings, whether from nature or from authority. Two young men from Egulac, a village on the southeast coast of Admiralty Island in the Alexander Archipelago of Southeast Alaska, went down to the river to hunt seals. They had a good supply of food and a strong canoe, and they were happy and carefree. Suddenly, without warning, a great wave came up and swept them away.
The water was unusually calm and still, with not a ripple on the surface. The fog was so thick that you couldn't see your hand in front of your face. The two young men paddled their canoe out to the middle of the river, where the hunting was best, and began to call for seals. They had barely finished their first call when they heard a loud crash.
A great wave had come up behind them, out of the fog, and it had swallowed their canoe. The two young men struggled to hold on, but the wave tossed them high in the air and then let them fall back into the cold water. They swam to the canoe, but before they could climb back in, another wave came and swept them away again.
This happened three times before the two young men finally climbed back in the canoe. But as soon as they did, a great wave crashed down and split the canoe in two. The two young men were left in the water, injured and exhausted, with nothing to hold onto.
Just then, a boat from Egulac appeared out of the fog. The captain of the boat had seen the two young men struggling in the water and had come to their rescue.

Historical context
Potlatching is a fundamental aspect of the Tlingit culture and a way of life that has existed for hundreds of years. Potlatching is not a single event, but a process by which goods and wealth are transferred between individuals, families, and groups. The concept of potlatching is rooted in the idea that all things belong to a larger community, and that individuals hold their possessions on a temporary basis. This idea is reflected in the Tlingit phrase "he who is rich, is my relative," which expresses the idea that what one person has, ultimately belongs to the community, and can be taken and redistributed as need be.
The act of potlatching involves a potlatch host who invites other potlatchers to a feast. The host gives away many of his possessions, including gold and silver, totem treasurers, canoes, and even land. In turn, the potlatchers bring gifts to the feast. Tornadoes at sea are rare, but they are more common than is generally believed. In fact, between 1999 and 2009 the Canadian government recorded 1,668 tornadoes over the country, and 10 percent of them occurred over the water.

How they form
Regular tornadoes form when warm, moist air rises rapidly in a thunderstorm, twisting and turning to form a funnel cloud. The twisting motion is produced by differences in wind speed and direction between the rising air and the air around it.
Tornadoes at sea form in a similar way, but the rising air is not in a thunderstorm. Instead, it is a massive bubble of warm water rising up from the ocean floor. This can happen when water is warmed by an underlying volcano or by the sun warms the water over a continental slope. The rising water creates a suction effect, drawing in more water and creating a whirlpool. If the water is turbid, a funnel cloud will form. If not, a waterspout will form. Either way, the result is a tornado at sea.

Maybe the people in the story are imagining what life was like before they had contact with Europeans. The story suggests that the people of long ago believed in the supernatural. The men were tired and decided to rest, even though this meant they missed the opportunity to catch the seals. == Transcription ==  The Tale of Tuna Kid  by George Bustin 

Once upon a time, in a far-off land, there was a great big river. And on this river there was a great big canoe, and in this canoe there were two young men from a village called Egulac. They had gone down to the river to hunt for seals, and they had their weapons ready. They were very quiet, and they paddled with all their might, for they did not want to scare the seals.

But suddenly it grew foggy, and calm

They heard a voice calling them from the edge of the fog bank. It was Aisanka, the seal woman, who invited them to come and live with her and the other sea people. The young men refused and fled back to the village as fast as they could. But they were pursued by the sea people and finally captured. Aisanka told them that they had offended her by refusing to come and live with her. She punished them by turning them into animals that could not speak or move.  Their bones were found later on the beach between Egulac and Tlowitz.

This is a tale from the Tlowitz First Nation, one of the tribes of the Kwakiutl people, of a sea woman named Aisanka who lived in the time before records were kept. There are several variations of this tale, but in all of them, people who offend the sea people are punished by being turned into animals. In some versions, the offenders are turned into lobsters or crabs. In others, they are turned into the bones that are later found on the beach.
